mural-en-clinica-dental-cordoba.title_en: MURAL PAINTING IN DENTIST PRACTICE, CORDOBA
text_en: Mural painted in a dental clinic in Córdoba, together with Víctor Barrios.
EASY
A project carried out with the support of the Fundación Botí in Córdoba for the open call ARTE CONTRA EL DESCONCIERTO.

Through the metaphorical power of kintsugi, Easy explores the technical and practical aspects of art and their conceptual connection by means of this intricate technique. The metaphorical force of kintsugi, together with its striking aesthetic, makes it a unique and powerful art form, one capable of touching our lives.

Easy is a reflection on the present historical moment and on how, out of the newly established order, new ways of thinking, of being and of existing in the world are emerging. It is also an optimistic look towards the future, and at how, from something that breaks, something even more interesting than what came before can be created. The practice of kintsugi, which enhances the beauty of scars, shows how this can be done with aesthetic and ethical canons adapted to the new situation we are living through at this moment.
Mixed media: ceramic, epoxy resin, mica powder and paint
Dimensions of the piece:

Diameter: 18.5 cm

Height: 5 cm

expo.title_en: Exhibition at Galatea Art Gallery.  Córdoba
text_en: The origins of landscape as a genre go back to the backgrounds of Renaissance paintings, from which it gently emerged as a staging for a mythological or biblical subject, or for some political episode. Over time these historical scenes receded into the background and began to give way to the depiction of landscape for its own sake. Today the aesthetics of landscape are expressed through a vocabulary of psychological and emotional states: bucolic, picturesque, exotic, sublime.

On an individual level, landscape is biographical: place is to landscape what identity is to portraiture. We are immersed in this medium, landscape, which is dynamic and sensory, and we inhabit and experience it with our bodies and our minds.

Today we live in a world full of digital images. The landscape we experience in our minds is a blend of the real one and the images we contemplate through the electronic devices that are ever-present in our lives. Ana Martínez's drawings and paintings are the result of a patient observation of these two visual stimuli that surround us, and they reflect how this shapes our experience of landscape.
In her work, Ana reverses the natural process from the real to the virtual, turning digital images into handmade ones, and creates landscapes that spring from the collective subconscious of our age.
‘In contrast to traditional art, modern art does not hide the fact that it is something made and produced: on the contrary, it emphasises it.’ Theodor W. Adorno.
I remember only the emotion of things,
and everything else I forget;
many are the gaps in my memory.
Antonio Machado

si-pudiese-entrar-en-tu-cabeza-aunque-fu.title_en: If only I could get inside your head at least for 5 minutes.
text_en: This piece was made for the project #Lo imposible. Lo inalcanzable, on autism and art, in which a group of artists, myself among them, worked with people with autism spectrum disorder.
The setting, the church of La Magdalena in Córdoba, was decisive in the conception of the work, owing to its aesthetic and historical weight.

I use the spiral of the winding staircase that leads up to the bell tower to make a journey into the head of Fran, an eight-year-old boy with autism who thrills to watching basketball games. In our imagination we enter through the cochlea of the inner ear, spiral-shaped just like the staircase, and make our way into his mind and his particular inner world. Something is happening there: a festival of the senses, only amplified by ASD. I wanted to recreate the sound of a basketball game and the multicoloured emotions Fran feels inside.

As we step into the staircase and witness the scene, I try to make possible the wish of his mother, who told me with a sigh: “If only I could get inside his head, even for just 5 minutes…!”

el-universo-de-fran-y-dani.title_en: The Universe of Fran and Dani
text_en: A workshop in which children with and without autism took part. The setting was the Church of La Magdalena, Córdoba. The workshop was one of the parallel activities of the project #LoimposibleLoinalcanzable, on art and autism (http://www.autismoyarte.com/ana-martinez_-fran-y-dani-hernandez/). Its aim was the inclusion of children with ASD and raising awareness among the other children so that they could learn about the specific nature of autism. Within the piece I created about the twins I worked with on this project, I proposed a free-drift workshop. First, we described to the non-autistic children the behaviour patterns of children affected by autism, to ease their interaction and help them become aware of these behaviours. Meanwhile the protagonists, Fran and Dani, the twins with autism, were getting tangled up playing with the blue ropes of the piece I had created for them. Then everyone played together, tangling themselves up further. Paula, another girl with autism, threw herself wholeheartedly into the game, and it was truly magical to see the children's naturalness and how the barriers came down.

In this workshop, held in the courtyards of the Palacio de Viana in Córdoba, we made a video piece taking as its starting point the sensory experience of the Palace courtyards. To do so, we divided the participants into five groups and asked each one to describe in images how each of the senses responded on the walk through the courtyards. We filmed everything with the tablets used as audio guides for visiting the courtyards museum. The result was surprising in its originality and freshness. Editing was by deBlur, and the wonderful photographs are courtesy of Joey Cuesta.

Held as part of the BioCórdoba organic food fair, in collaboration with Almocafre, the Córdoba organic produce cooperative. A group of children created a free-form painting using organic vegetables and seeds as their colours. The result was an ephemeral and visually beautiful work, which we enjoyed tasting at the end of the workshop.
White paint, covering almost the entire surface of the canvas, gradually cuts out the figures in an exercise of repainting what has already been painted; here the background takes centre stage.

Cribs is an installation made up of six hospital cribs, each containing a light box with Cibachrome photographs.

Each photograph shows an adult lying in bed, in an intimate, relaxed pose. The piece is a reflection on the private domains of the human being in solitude. Above all, Cribs is meant as a deliberately ironic nod to a concept as socially accepted as adult maturity.

Public Windows grows out of a reflection on the different ways of understanding privacy, on what we show and what we hide, depending on the cultural setting and religious tradition of each place, or on its customs. Coming, in my case, from an Arab heritage, from the south of Spain, where everything that happens behind closed doors is jealously guarded, it is a great surprise to see how in northern Europe the most intimate moments of domestic life are exposed to the outside without the slightest modesty. In this piece, which represents a residential block in northern Europe, the private life of its inhabitants is displayed as if it were a shop window. Each of the images, in a format inspired by the windows of Amsterdam's buildings, presents an everyday domestic moment in which the protagonists, oblivious to the voyeur's gaze, feel no discomfort at being watched.

Project carried out during an Erasmus residency at the Rietveld Akademie, Amsterdam.

2 Kates is a double portrait. The two sitters share a name, Kate, and a city in northern Europe. Two women who, in the portrait, represent two very different realities.

One Kate is Nigerian, an illegal resident in Amsterdam, and underage. She has come to Europe, the dreamed-of paradise for so many sub-Saharan Africans. She has herself photographed with the media icons of our time: famous models, fashion brands, the illuminated billboards on bus shelters all over the city. Her dreamed-of references are not historical monuments or landmarks, but people who embody a sociocultural ideal of success, of the developed world, of Europe.

The other Kate, the model on the billboard, is a product of consumer society and represents the Western beauty ideals of the modern world.

The African Kate is the product of a world that trades in people. She works as a prostitute in a district where she is displayed in a kind of shop-window cell, and with what she manages to earn she will never be able to pay off her debt to the mafia that brought her to Europe.

Kate Moss is a public figure with a well-known name and face, unlike Kate, who is anonymous, like so many others who share her situation.

2 Kates starts from a reflection on the role of two radically different women who, paradoxically, have something in common: woman as an object of consumer society, on different levels.

Project carried out during an Erasmus residency at the Rietveld Akademie, Amsterdam.
